news.title: This Star-Studded Progressive Event Featuring James Talarico and Kamala Harris Was a Complete Flop
news.text:
The Democrat Party’s youth movement appears to be in complete shambles as the DemocracySummit 2026, what was slated to be a “a powerful day of organizing, learning, and civic renewal,” had absolutely abysmal attendance in Austin, Texas.

This is how many people wanted to hear to @SenMarkKelly speak today at the nation’s largest progressive youth conferenceZero media are reporting on this disaster.When we have tens of thousands of people at our events they report on minor little things.Crickets for libs pic.twitter.com/eD35JW6KEH— Tyler Bowyer (@tylerbowyer) August 16, 2026

Turnout at the 2026 Democracy Summit in Austin was low. A mostly empty room when Kamala Harris gave her remarks. pic.twitter.com/rdbZVd7yQI— Tony Ortiz (Current Revolt) (@CurrentRevolt) August 18, 2026

Despite boasting a star-studded slate of progressive speakers like former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sens. Mark Kelly and Chris Murphy, Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, and Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin, the venue appeared to be completely empty.

Footage uploaded to social media by Turning Point executive Tyler Bowyer showed a near-empty room during remarks delivered by Democrat Mark Kelly, who many have pushed as a potential dark horse in the 2028 presidential primaries. Another video published by Current Revolt seemed to indicate that right-wing comedian Alex Stein drew the largest crowd of the event following a debate with progressive streamer Destiney.

The startlingly poor attendance for a progressive event, one hosted deep in the heart of Talarico country, is an ominous sign for Democrats who hope to flip Texas despite questionable polls that claim razor-thin margins in the red state.

news.title: Trump's Approval is Dropping with Millennials, New Poll Shows
news.text: President Donald Trump's approval rating among millennials is slipping in the latest Economist/YouGov poll, adding to a broader pattern of declining support among younger Americans. Just 26 percent of those age 30 to 44, or millennials, now approve of the job Trump is doing as president, according to the poll conducted from August 14 until August 17. That is down from 29 percent last week and marks the fifth consecutive week in which his approval among the group has declined or held steady. The new poll also found Trump's overall approval at 35 percent, with 61 percent disapproving of his job performance. The poll surveyed 1,611 U.S. adults and has a margin of error of 3.4 percent. White House Spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Newsweek via email when asked about the new poll on Tuesday, "President Trump has signed the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, driven violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs. President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess and there is more work to do, but the United States of America has never been stronger.” A White House official also pointed Newsweek to policy-related achievements this week, including what the administration described as the largest drop in violent crime in American history, with FBI data showing violent crime fell over 9 percent in 2025. The official also pointed to 15 consecutive months of zero migrant releases at the border, a notable decline in apprehensions, and a 3.1 percent year-over-year drop in prescription drug prices in July — the steepest annual decline in more than 60 years, according to The Washington Post. Why Millennial Votes Matter Millennials are defined generally as people born from 1981 to 1996. The generation has overtaken the baby boomers as the largest age demographic, according to the Pew Research Center. Parallel efforts by both Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris' campaigns to reach millennials via podcasts and other digital media emerged as a key feature of the 2024 campaign cycle. What To Know The Economist/YouGov poll also shows that younger Americans are particularly negative about several areas of Trump's presidency. Among voters ages 18 to 29, just 30 percent approve of Trump's overall job performance while 67 percent disapprove. Among those ages 30 to 44, 26 percent approve and 70 percent disapprove. The same poll found only 24 percent of 18-to-29-year-olds approve of Trump's handling of foreign policy, while 25 percent approve of his handling of tariffs. Millennials' approval of those policy issues is further underwater, with 21 percent approving of the president's handling of foreign policy and 19 percent approving of his handling of tariffs. The last time the president's approval with the key voting bloc was 26 percent or below was in a survey taken from June 5-8 by the pollster, where the president's approval with millennials was 26 percent. The numbers come as Trump approaches the 2026 midterm elections with his overall approval at or near its lowest. YouGov reported earlier this month that 33 percent of Americans approved of Trump's job performance, while 62 percent disapproved — the highest disapproval rating recorded for him in the poll. The latest 35 percent approval figure is a slight improvement from that reading, but the decline among younger voters remains a notable part of Trump's broader polling picture. Map Shows Trump's Approval Slipping with Millennials What Other Polls Show An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Trump's overall approval rating is 40 percent compared to a 59 percent disapproval rating. Among 18–34-year-olds, Trump's approval is 28 percent, and his disapproval rating is 72 percent. Among those aged 35 to 49, his approval rating is 40 percent, and his disapproval rating is 57 percent. The poll surveyed 1,002 registered voters in the likely electorate from August 13-17 and has a margin of error of 3.4 percent. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday shows Trump's overall approval rating is 33 percent and his disapproval rating is 64 percent. The poll surveyed 1,166 U.S. adults from August 14-17, 2026, and has a margin of error of 3 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The numbers come as Trump approaches the 2026 midterm elections with his overall approval at or near its lowest

news.title: CBS’s 60 Minutes adds another high-profile hire after firings and exits
news.text:
Ariel Levy, a staff writer for The New Yorker, is joining “60 Minutes” as a contributor, CBS News announced Monday. 

The move marks the latest addition to the news program following a sweeping overhaul led by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss.

In a memo sent to newsroom staff, newly appointed Executive Producer Nick Bilton praised Levy’s career, which includes nearly 30 years covering culture, gender and health.

“Ariel is an astonishingly original writer and reporter, fearlessly going to far-flung places and exploring sensitive topics that have driven consequential debates,” Bilton wrote. “For nearly three decades, first at New York magazine and then at The New Yorker, she has reported on culture, gender, sexuality, health and the people and ideas shaping modern life in a way that is entirely unique.”

Levy has served as a staff writer at The New Yorker since 2008, where her work ranged from analyzing the “Girls Gone Wild” franchise to profiling major political and cultural figures. She is also the author of “Female Chauvinist Pigs” and the memoir “The Rules Do Not Apply.”

In 2014, Levy received a National Magazine Award for her deeply personal essay, “Thanksgiving in Mongolia”, which detailed suffering a miscarriage the previous year while five months pregnant during a reporting trip to the country.

Her arrival comes as the news program works to rebuild its roster ahead of its 59th season premiere on Sept. 13. 

“Ariel adds to our truly exceptional group of correspondents and contributors for Season 59,” Bilton said. “They bring different journalism backgrounds, experiences, interests and ways of telling stories, but they share the qualities that matter here: curiosity, independence, incredible reporting, a willingness to hold power to account, and an instinct for the kind of stories people can’t stop watching.”

Bilton previously brought on conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat, author Sebastian Junger, CBS News correspondent Trevor Phillips and filmmaker Gianna Toboni in July. They join returning correspondents Lesley Stahl, Jon Wertheim, Bill Whitaker and Norah O’Donnell.

The hiring spree follows a series of high-profile departures. Weiss pushed out former Executive Producer Tanya Simon, executive editor Draggan Mihailovich, and correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega in late May. Anchor Scott Pelley departed shortly after, following a disagreement with Bilton, while Anderson Cooper left earlier in the year over concerns regarding the network's direction under Weiss.

Weiss has sought to reshape “60 Minutes” to attract younger and digital-first audiences, while advocating for broader coverage of Trump administration officials and conservative viewpoints.

The editorial shifts come amid internal strain following Paramount’s settlement of a $16 million lawsuit with the Trump administration over a pre-election interview conducted by Whitaker with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The legal battle and subsequent settlement, reached as Paramount finalized its sale to Skydance, prompted the resignations of senior CBS News executives Bill Owens and Wendy McMahon.

The financial stakes remain high for the network. Data from iSpot indicates “60 Minutes” generated roughly $67 million to $69 million in advertising revenue in both 2024 and 2025, driven largely by major pharmaceutical sponsors including Rinvoq, Skyrizi, Claritin and Vabysmo.

However, the abrupt restructuring has compressed production timelines for the upcoming season, leaving fewer staff members to develop segments during the summer months, as reported by Variety.
news.summary: With the new season set to premiere Sept. 13, the broadcast team faces a compressed summer production schedule

news.title: AOC Overtakes Gavin Newsom in 2028 Odds as Democrats Shift Left
news.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has moved to the front of the field among potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders on prediction markets, overtaking California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

The 36-year-old New York progressive, widely known as AOC, has seen a recent burst of backing on online markets including Kalshi and Polymarket.

Her rise has pushed Newsom out of the top slot, with Kalshi placing her chances of winning the 2028 Democratic nomination at 18 percent and Polymarket putting her at 19 percent.

Newsom had been the market favorite since the betting lines were first launched.

Ocasio-Cortez’s momentum may reflect growing energy on the party’s left flank, as Democratic Socialist candidates gain traction in races across the country.

Still, the shift in prediction odds stands in sharp contrast to what traditional polling currently shows.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris remains the leader in national surveys measuring support for the next Democratic presidential nominee, according to polls released this month.

A Rasmussen poll found Harris with 37 percent support among likely Democratic primary voters, an increase from 34 percent in May.

The same poll showed Newsom had 14 percent, former Transportation Secretary and 2020 presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg had the backing of 10 percent of respondents and AOC had 9 percent. 

None of the Democratic hopefuls have actually announced a bid for the White House.

Still, AOC has been leaning into her recent surge in popularity. 

Pressed on the possibility of launching a presidential bid in the next contest earlier this month, AOC told ABC News: ‘I haven’t ruled out the possibility.’

‘And I’m very humbled by the tremendous amount of support out there,’ she added. 

What sets AOC apart from the pack of serious 2028 contenders is her social media acumen, history of pushing progressive policies as the party veers leftward and massive name recognition nationwide. 

She recently went viral for her candid videos about freezing her eggs, sparking a debate online about women’s reproductive rights, as well as speculation about her private life.

AOC and her longtime partner Riley Roberts called off their engagement in February, Our News Outlet revealed last week. Neither AOC nor Roberts have publicly confirmed the breakup before her posts about fertility treatment.

Their relationship appeared to become increasingly strained as AOC’s political career exploded while Roberts remained largely behind the scenes, sources said. 

The split comes as AOC is hoping to ride a progressive wave carved out by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, as well as progressive candidate victories in Michigan and Minnesota, where Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan each won contested primaries against centrist opponents.

After hosting rallies around the country last year with Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, himself a progressive icon, the New York lawmaker appears poised to receive the mantle from him. 

While rallying with Sanders during their ‘Fight the Oligarchy’ tour during Trump’s first months back in office, the Senator joked that AOC was his ‘daughter,’ and the Congresswoman reciprocated, referring to him as her uncle.

news.title: Disney, ABC sue US regulator over threat to broadcast licences
news.text:
Disney and ABC accused the Trump administration of increasing pressure on ABC, culminating in threats to the broadcasting licences of its stations. (EPA Images pic)
WASHINGTON: Walt Disney-owned ABC sued the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Tuesday, accusing the US regulatory body of waging a retaliatory campaign against the television network on behalf of the Trump administration.
The lawsuit, filed in a federal district court in Washington, comes after the FCC earlier this year asked ABC TV stations to renew their broadcast licences earlier than scheduled.
"Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts," the suit says.
"Over time, those attacks have escalated into express demands that ABC be stripped of its broadcast licences because of its speech."
President Donald Trump has personally lashed out at ABC – particularly the network's late night host Jimmy Kimmel – on numerous occasions and suggested revoking the broadcast licences of stations he claims are "almost 100% negative" towards him.
The famously litigious Republican president has filed a number of defamation lawsuits against media outlets, including suing ABC over statements about a civil judgement in a sexual assault case.
He took CBS to court for allegedly misleading viewers by airing different clips of the same answer from an interview with 2024 Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.
The cases involving ABC and CBS ended in December 2024 and July 2025, with the broadcasters promising to pay US$15 million and US$16 million, respectively.
Other ongoing cases include a US$10 billion lawsuit against the BBC over an allegedly misleading edit of one of his speeches and one against The Wall Street Journal over publication of a salacious birthday letter he allegedly sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
'Government intimidation'
In its lawsuit filed on Tuesday, Disney and ABC said the Trump administration has "steadily increased the pressure on ABC, culminating in the present threat to the broadcasting licenses of the eight ABC Owned Stations.
"The Commission has demanded a review of the Stations' licenses extraordinarily early," it says. "That timing underscores the Commission's true purpose: coercing and retaliating against a network that refuses to bow to the Administration's demands."
"Facing this existential threat, Plaintiffs have no choice but to seek redress from the judicial branch for the Administration's blatant retaliation for their First Amendment speech," the suit says.
ABC and Disney asked the court to issue a restraining order preventing the FCC from taking any action against the network's broadcasting licences, which were not up for renewal until 2028.
Anna Gomez, the sole commissioner on the FCC appointed by a Democratic president, welcomed the lawsuit as pushback against what she called "government intimidation."
"For months, the FCC has waged a campaign of censorship and control against Disney's ABC stations, using the threat of broadcast license revocations to punish a company for speech this administration doesn't like," Gomez said in a statement.
"It is time this administration understands that the Constitution does not bend to political convenience, and that the First Amendment protects the news and commentary Americans see on their screens even when those in power wish it didn't," she added.
news.summary: The lawsuit comes after the FCC earlier this year asked ABC TV stations to renew their broadcast licences earlier than scheduled.

news.title: Democrats’ Push for Generational Change Could Hit a Wall in Massachusetts
news.text: Senator Ed Markey led Representative Seth Moulton in two new polls of the Democratic Senate primary in Massachusetts, as the longtime incumbent seeks to hold off another generational challenge. An anti-incumbent wave has swept through the Democratic primaries ahead of the midterms, with several longtime members of Congress losing to political newcomers. Markey, 80, has drawn a challenge from Moulton, 47, who has argued it is time for new leadership in the Bay State. Democrats have been confronting questions about the age of some of their top politicians over the past few years. Those calls grew after backlash over former President Joe Biden’s decision to run for a second term despite age concerns that grew after a debate against President Donald Trump in June 2024 that eventually led to his withdrawal. The debate was seen as a pivotal turning point in the election that boosted Trump’s campaign to return to the White House. Although many Democrats want fewer octogenarians and a new generation of leadership, Markey appears well-positioned to fend off the challenge from Moulton, according to new polls from the University of Massachusetts Amherst and Suffolk University released this week. While Moulton has sought to make the race about Markey's age and has emphasized calls for new leadership, Markey has focused on the ideological and policy differences between the two, casting himself as more in line with voters on issues like health care. Markey is viewed as one of the most progressive senators in office, while Moulton is a moderate who has criticized the party on transgender rights and has not supported Medicare for All. Markey's focus on his progressive bona fides makes the race unique from other contentious primaries, where challengers have more often been more progressive than incumbents. Markey supporters believe a race defined by ideology, not age, could benefit him in such a progressive state. Ed Markey Leads Two New Polls Markey has built up a consistent polling lead over Moulton, who currently represents a district based around Massachusetts’ North Shore. Markey has served in the United States Senate since 2013 and previously served in Congress since 1976. Moulton has represented his district since 2015. The UMass Amherst poll showed Markey with a wide lead over Moulton, holding a 28-point advantage, 60 percent to 32 percent when leaners were pushed. It surveyed 800 registered voters, including 445 Democratic primary voters, from August 5-12, 2026. The Suffolk poll showed a closer race but still gave Markey a 15-point advantage, 52 percent to 38 percent, with 10 percent undecided. It surveyed 500 likely voters from August 13-16, 2026, and was sponsored by The Boston Globe. Tatishe Nteta, professor of political science and director of the UMass poll, told Newsweek that it would be difficult for Moulton to unseat Markey, whose approval rating remains in the 80s among Democratic primary voters. “You need to provide a real reason as to why there needs to be a change in leadership. To date, the only reason that Representative Moulton has provided is Senator Markey’s age, his long tenure in the U.S. Congress and the need for generational change,” he said. “What our polling is showing, as well as the polling of Suffolk and others, is that that’s not resonating with the Democratic electorate.” Taylor Hebble, a spokesperson for Moulton, told Newsweek that public polling “has a recent history of being wildly wrong.” “Just look at Wisconsin and Michigan, where double-digit polling leads evaporated on Election Day. If you want to know how this race is going, look at Ed Markey’s recent actions: He is skipping candidate forums and taking $62,000 from Chuck Schumer – away from battleground races. Massachusetts is ready for change,” Hebble said. Newsweek reached out to Markey’s campaign for comment via his press contact form. Why Ed Markey May Defeat Generational Challenge Several older incumbent Democrats in places like New York, Colorado and Connecticut have lost to younger challengers, many of whom are anti-establishment and more progressive. But the dynamics of this race are different, according to experts. “Here, instead of the upstart challenger being young and progressive and the incumbent being more moderate, if not a member of the establishment wing of the Democratic Party, we have a senator who is older and viewed by many voters as the more progressive candidate. But also, who has clear progressive bona fides,” he said. Markey has emphasized his support for progressive policies like the Green New Deal and Medicare for All on the campaign trail, while Moulton’s past comments opposing the inclusion of transgender athletes in girls’ sports have come up as an issue for him in polling, Nteta said. Costas Panagopoulos, professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek Markey is an “institution” in Massachusetts but that many voters do have reservations about his age. Markey will be hard to beat, but it is not impossible, he said. “Ideologically, [Markey] is perceived to be to the left of Moulton, and given that primary voters tend to be more ideologically extreme than in general elections, this is a case in which it might serve Markey well,” he said. He noted that Moulton is also not quite viewed as an outsider, having served in the House of Representatives for a decade. “Voters may not be viewing him as a non-incumbent as other candidates across the country who have been able to ride that anti-incumbent, anti-establishment wave have managed to do,” he said. Markey has been able to beat generational challenges in the past. In 2020, then-Representative Joe Kennedy III ran against Markey in the Democratic primary on a platform of generational change, but Markey won that race by nearly 10 points. He did so by unifying more progressive voters in the solidly blue state, winning endorsements from top progressives. He also won support among younger Democrats, who helped build his social media presence on the “Markeyverse,” a network of meme accounts that supported his reelection. Still, Moulton is well-known across the state and garnered national attention when he ran a longshot bid for president in 2020 but struggled to gain momentum over more well-known candidates. Some voters have welcomed his calls for new leadership, but his more moderate policies may not be playing as well with progressives in the state. For instance, Moulton faced backlash from many Democrats last year over remarks about transgender athletes in an interview with The New York Times. He said at the time, “I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” What Do Other Polls Show? Some other recent polls suggest a closer race. A University of New Hampshire poll, which surveyed 367 likely voters from June 18-23, 2026, showed Markey up 6 points, 41 percent to 35 percent. An earlier Emerson College poll, which surveyed 451 likely voters from May 3-4, showed Markey up 5 points, 37 percent to 32 percent. Moulton’s Path to Victory Panagopoulos said he believes there is still a path to victory for Moulton in Massachusetts if he is able to mobilize his base of voters, as primaries often come down to turnout. His campaign needs to spend the coming weeks making their case “effectively” and harping on its strengths, including the generational change argument. “Turnout is going to be crucial in this election because primaries tend to attract fewer voters, and the composition of the electorate will matter tremendously in this primary for the two candidates involved,” he said. Nteta said politics can sometimes “surprise you” and that “anything can happen” in the final weeks. Moulton could benefit if he is perceived as more engaged and energetic in the final debate against Markey or if he is able to win over more moderate voters in the state. He said it’s an “uphill climb” for Moulton but that anything is possible in the closing weeks of the campaign. What Happens Next The primary is set for September 1, 2026. Attorney John Deaton is viewed as the presumptive Republican nominee, but the general election is viewed as less competitive. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Massachusetts in 2024 by 25 points over President Donald Trump, and the environment is widely expected to favor Democrats by analysts due to Trump’s declining national approval rating. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as safe or solid for Democrats. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Senator Ed Markey leads polls against Rep. Seth Moulton, who has argued for generational change in the Massachusetts Senate race.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Polling Company Says It Faked Survey Data in Los Angeles and Wisconsin Races
news.text:
A fake polling company that released polls in Los Angeles and Wisconsin races this month said on Aug. 17 that it fabricated its data as part of a “social experiment” project.

“Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” the company posted on its now-defunct website.

The entity has declined to identify who operated the website and the fake polling company and didn’t respond to The Epoch Times’ request for information.

All surveys and data were removed from the site on Aug. 18.

“All previously published polling releases have been withdrawn and should not be cited or treated as genuine polling data,” Median Strategies stated.

The disclosure prompted Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass’s reelection campaign to remove a social media post cheering the Median Strategies poll results released Aug. 12 showing she led challenger Nithya Raman by 11 points.

Bass’s campaign didn’t respond to a request for comment but told the Los Angeles Times that “any bad faith attempts to influence elections should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Raman’s campaign also didn’t respond to a request for comment but, in comments to the Times, criticized Bass for failing to research the polling company before sharing the results.

Bass’s financial records showed she did pay $67,250 for polling and research from David Binder Research in San Francisco, according to her latest campaign report ending June 30.

Binder is a longtime campaign strategist of former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama. Binder was one of the first people Obama called when he decided to run for president, his former strategist Davide Axelrod told ABC News.

In another fake poll this month, a Median Strategies survey claimed Wisconsin Rep. Francesca Hong led Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley by 23 points in the Democratic primary for governor on Aug. 11.

The candidates didn’t advertise the poll on their social media platforms.

State Navigate, a left-leaning news outlet, also conducted a poll in the same Wisconsin governor’s race that had similar results, showing Hong with a 22-point lead four days before the primary election.

Michael Foley, an elections coordinator with State Navigate, told The Epoch Times the polling company conducted its own research and wasn’t affiliated with Median Strategies.

“State Navigate wasn’t influenced by and had nothing to do with Median Strategies’ fake poll, and we actually painstakingly conducted all the polls listed on our report card and elsewhere on our website ourselves,” Foley said in an email.

Los Angeles Times reporter Noah Goldberg was the first to break the news about the bogus pollsters after trying to reach out to them last week.

Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, who was edged out of the top two spots in the primary, commented on the fabricated poll.

The company also stated no individuals involved with Median Strategies received compensation or financial benefit from the project, which was apparently not funded, commissioned, or directed by a candidate, campaign, political party, political action committee, media organization, or outside entity.

news.title: Polling Company Says It Faked Survey Data in Los Angeles and Wisconsin Races
news.text:
A fake polling company that released polls in Los Angeles and Wisconsin races this month said on Aug. 17 that it fabricated its data as part of a “social experiment” project.

“Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” the company posted on its now-defunct website.

The entity has declined to identify who operated the website and the fake polling company and didn’t respond to The Epoch Times’ request for information.

All surveys and data were removed from the site on Aug. 18.

“All previously published polling releases have been withdrawn and should not be cited or treated as genuine polling data,” Median Strategies stated.

The disclosure prompted Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass’s reelection campaign to remove a social media post cheering the Median Strategies poll results released Aug. 12 showing she led challenger Nithya Raman by 11 points.

Bass’s campaign didn’t respond to a request for comment but told the Los Angeles Times that “any bad faith attempts to influence elections should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Raman’s campaign also didn’t respond to a request for comment but, in comments to the Times, criticized Bass for failing to research the polling company before sharing the results.

Bass’s financial records showed she did pay $67,250 for polling and research from David Binder Research in San Francisco, according to her latest campaign report ending June 30.

Binder is a longtime campaign strategist of former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama. Binder was one of the first people Obama called when he decided to run for president, his former strategist Davide Axelrod told ABC News.

In another fake poll this month, a Median Strategies survey claimed Wisconsin Rep. Francesca Hong led Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley by 23 points in the Democratic primary for governor on Aug. 11.

The candidates didn’t advertise the poll on their social media platforms.

State Navigate, a left-leaning news outlet, also conducted a poll in the same Wisconsin governor’s race that had similar results, showing Hong with a 22-point lead four days before the primary election.

Michael Foley, an elections coordinator with State Navigate, told The Epoch Times the polling company conducted its own research and wasn’t affiliated with Median Strategies.

“State Navigate wasn’t influenced by and had nothing to do with Median Strategies’ fake poll, and we actually painstakingly conducted all the polls listed on our report card and elsewhere on our website ourselves,” Foley said in an email.

Los Angeles Times reporter Noah Goldberg was the first to break the news about the bogus pollsters after trying to reach out to them last week.

Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, who was edged out of the top two spots in the primary, commented on the fabricated poll.

The company also stated no individuals involved with Median Strategies received compensation or financial benefit from the project, which was apparently not funded, commissioned, or directed by a candidate, campaign, political party, political action committee, media organization, or outside entity.

The project also claimed it was not involved in election prediction markets, betting markets, or other schemes tied to races covered in its polls.

news.title: Jon Ossoff's 2028 Chances As He Takes Aim at Trump Aide Natalie Harp
news.text: Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking reelection this November in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, has also drawn speculation as a potential Democratic contender in the 2028 presidential election. During a recent Senate campaign speech, Ossoff criticized President Donald Trump over his policy priorities and specifically referenced Natalie Harp's close role in the president's orbit. Following those comments, prediction markets have shifted Ossoff's standing among potential 2028 Democratic presidential nominees, with some markets showing his standing has slipped while others show it has risen after his comments. Ossoff has repeatedly dismissed speculation about a 2028 presidential run, saying his focus remains on Georgia's Senate race and the upcoming midterm elections. Newsweek has reached out to Ossoff’s campaign for comment via email on Tuesday. Prediction Markets Change Ossoff's 2028 Presidential Chances Prediction market Kalshi gave Ossoff a 14 percent chance of securing the Democratic presidential nomination early on the morning of August 16, the same day he made the remarks. By Tuesday afternoon, those odds had risen to 16 percent. On Polymarket, however, Ossoff’s odds have slightly slipped since his comments. The market put his odds at securing the Democratic nomination on August 16 morning at 14.8 percent. As of Tuesday afternoon, the market puts his odds at 14 percent. Both markets put him behind Representative Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, and Polymarket finds him behind California Governor Gavin Newsom, while Kalshi finds the two politicians tied. What Has Ossoff Said About Running For President? With no major Democrat yet publicly entering the 2028 presidential race, attention remains centered on the November midterms, including Ossoff's closely watched reelection bid in Georgia, as both parties battle for control of the Senate. Ossoff has acknowledged that his reelection bid remains competitive, even as he has amassed a substantial campaign war chest. Ossoff reported about $42 million cash on hand, nearly 20 times the amount reported by his opponent, Republican Mike Collins, according to a recent Federal Election Commission (FEC) filing in July. On Monday, he told MS Now's Jen Psaki, “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now.” “These midterms are the whole ballgame,” Ossoff said, adding, “I don't know that we have a free and fair election in 2028 unless we restore checks and balances in these 2026 midterm elections. This needs to be all of our highest priority and focus.” Ossoff made similar remarks in April, when he told MS NOW's The Briefing that he had "zero interest" in a 2028 presidential campaign. "I love serving the state of Georgia. I've got two young daughters," he said. What Did Jon Ossoff Say About Trump Aide Natalie Harp? Ossoff singled out Harp by name at a campaign rally on Sunday, accusing Trump of preferring to "travel with Natalie" instead of doing his job. He told the Atlanta crowd, "While the sailors on the [U.S.S Abraham] Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. "He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn't want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie [Harp] on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar,” he told the audience about Trump, which erupted into applause. Top aides often travel with the president. A clip of Ossoff's speech had been viewed more than 6 million times as of Tuesday. Some Democrats have pushed for more visibility on the matter, while some Republicans, such as former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, wrote in part in an X post, "Jon Ossoff owes Natalie Harp a personal apology for having smeared her. If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job." Members of the administration have responded to Ossoff's comments by speaking about Harp's character, such as Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, who said on X Monday, "Natalie Harp is an incredibly hardworking, talented, principled, and loyal member of the Trump Admin who passionately wants to help our nation thrive. Every day, she brings drive and focus to her work serving our country. She’s truly a phenomenal member of POTUS’ team." Asked Monday by MS Now's Jen Psaki why the Georgia Senator mentioned Harp specifically, Ossoff said he had heard the aide described as Trump's "security blanket" and argued that senior staff is “not telling him [Trump] what he needs to hear. They're telling him what he wants to hear, and the nation is at war, and we cannot afford that." Ossoff continued: "We need a team in the White House. We need folks at the State Department, at the Defense Department, in the United States Congress, who take their jobs seriously. Those sailors out on the Lincoln, they do their jobs with excellence and dedication every single day. They didn't sign up for luxury. They signed up to defend the country.” He went on, “And the president, surrounded by enablers in the West Wing, is playing golf, is trading stock and is decorating his ballroom. It's a disgrace, all while American families in Georgia and across the country pay more for just about everything as a direct result of his failed economic policy and his failed foreign policy." What Has The White House Said About Natalie Harp? In a statement shared with Newsweek for a related story, White House spokesman Davis Ingle criticized Ossoff's record and rhetoric. “Jon Ossoff is a feminine theater kid who voted to massively raise taxes, give illegal immigrants free taxpayer-funded healthcare, and defund federal immigration enforcement and Border Patrol. Lightweight Jon’s rhetoric is cringeworthy, but his extreme voting record is dangerous,” he said. Trump has been asked about the remarks. On Monday, he dismissed Ossoff as a “Pee-wee Herman" lookalike and did not directly address the substance of the comment, instead pivoting to defend his White House ballroom construction project as a security and infrastructure upgrade while speaking in the Oval Office. CNN correspondent Kristen Holmes asked Trump in the Oval Office to respond to Ossoff's remarks, to which the president repeatedly told her to be quiet and called her "a fake reporter." Hours later, the official White House Rapid Response account posted on X that Holmes' children would one day be "sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive,” drawing condemnation from journalists and former Trump aides, including Sarah Matthews, a deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first term. On Monday, Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, reposted a clip of Ossoff's remarks on X and wrote, "Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he's a miserable person who hates this country. It's because he's a radical, extremist Dumocrat." What We Know About Natalie Harp Harp, 35, first came to Trump's attention in 2019, when she credited a federal right-to-try law he signed with giving her access to experimental treatment for stage 2 bone cancer. He invited her to join his 2020 campaign advisory board and to speak at that year's Republican National Convention. She worked as a presenter for One America News Network from 2020 to 2022 before joining Trump's 2024 campaign. She had earned her MBA from Liberty University in 2015. During the campaign, Harp earned the nickname "human printer" for carrying a portable printer so she could hand Trump paper copies of news articles, a habit that grew out of his preference for reading news on paper rather than a screen. She has also posted to Trump's Truth Social account on his behalf, a role that has continued since he named her executive assistant to the president in January 2025. Harp's father, an estate agent who founded a consultancy for travel companies, died by suicide in 2020. After his death, she and her brother became estranged, the latter said. Multiple outlets, including The New York Times, have reported concerns about Harp's relationship with Trump. The Secret Service reportedly came to view her as a security consideration, while aides, including incoming chief of staff Susie Wiles, were reportedly unsettled by her access, according to the new book Regime Change, by journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Sarah Matthews, a deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first term, echoed those reports Monday, saying it was fair to point out that Harp's closeness to Trump had “alarmed” the Secret Service. Harp was also one of three aides, along with Dan Scavino and Walt Nauta, who accompanied Trump on a decoy military flight out of Turkey last month amid a reported security threat. What Polls Show About Potential 2028 Democratic Candidates The latest poll from Focaldata and the Financial Times showed Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Governor Gavin Newsom and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez with the most significant share of votes. It found Harris in the lead with 30 percent, followed by Newsom at 14 percent, Buttigieg at 10 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 8 percent. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro followed at 6 percent, while Ossoff and Senator Mark Kelly each received 5 percent in the poll, which surveyed 2,152 adults August 7-11. An Emerson College Poll last month showed Buttigieg with 19 percent and Newsom with 17 percent. Ossoff had 13 percent, Ocasio-Cortez had 13 percent, Harris had 8 percent, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear had 7 percent, Governor Josh Shapiro landed 5 percent, and 13 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from July 19 to July 20, 2026, among 574 respondents and had a margin of error of 4 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas

news.title: Fox News Predicts Two Key GOP-Held Senate Seats Shifting Toward Democrats
news.text: Democrats' chances of flipping two Republican-held Senate seats have improved, according to Fox News' latest electoral rankings, boosting the party's prospects of reclaiming control of the chamber in November. The updated rankings shift the Senate races in Kansas and Texas, signaling a more competitive landscape in two states Democrats are eyeing in their path to secure a Senate majority. Democrats face a difficult map in 2026, needing to gain four seats while defending their own incumbents. The party has pointed to voter concerns over the economy, the ongoing Iran war, and President Donald Trump’s slipping approval rating as potential opportunities to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory. Republicans have a 53-47 majority in the Senate currently. While Democrats have seen improved odds in Kansas and Texas, according to Fox News, the party has lost ground in Michigan, according to the same forecast, which moved the race from "Lean Democrat" to "Toss Up." The competing shifts highlight the fluid nature of the battle for Senate control, with both parties facing increasingly competitive races across the map as the November election approaches. Alex Patton, a Republican political consultant, owner of Ozean Media, and political pollster, told Newsweek in an email that the recent forecasts indicate “Republicans are in a worse position,” adding that “economic conditions combined with deteriorating Presidential approval numbers are moving from a headwind to a tropical storm warning, approaching hurricane watch status.” Newsweek has reached out to the campaigns in Texas, Kansas, and Michigan for comment via email on Tuesday. What To Know A series of high-profile primaries in recent months have reshaped the map, elevating new candidates and prompting several major election forecasters to revisit their ratings. In some states, progressive candidates emerged victorious, including former Michigan health official Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Democratic nomination against Representative Haley Stevens earlier this month. Elsewhere, establishment-backed candidates have prevailed. Candidate shakeups have also altered the Senate map recently. In Texas, Ken Paxton's primary defeat of Senator John Cornyn heightened uncertainty in a race once seen as a more reliable Republican hold. In Alaska, Republicans have raised concerns that a candidate sharing Senator Dan Sullivan's name could complicate the incumbent's reelection bid, while in Maine, Democrat Graham Platner exited the race following controversy surrounding his campaign. With fewer than 100 days until Election Day, candidates are ramping up their efforts to mobilize voters in what is expected to be a closely watched fight for control of the Senate. For Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns and a Republican strategist, "Candidate quality is deciding toss-ups more than the national political environment," he told Newsweek. On Texas, he said that "[Ken] Paxton's fraud indictment, his impeachment trial, and a divorce filing amid affair allegations make Texas as much a referendum on him as on his party. But James Talarico is still very much the underdog given Texas' solid red bent. For Michigan, he said the race will be determined by turnout. "El-Sayed has to rebuild Black voter support in Detroit that's running well behind 2020 levels. Mike Rogers can't afford a repeat of the late Democratic surge that beat him in 2024," he added. Texas Senate Race The GOP's decadeslong hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico nearly deadlocked in polls. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Fox News updated its Senate ratings to move Texas into the "toss up" column, joining competitive races in Michigan, Iowa, Ohio, Maine and Alaska. However, The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball still rate the race as “leans Republican.” Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup comes after Paxton defeated longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. However, polls appear to flip-flop on who is leading, as a recent Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters puts the Senate race in a near dead heat, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. RealClearPolling aggregate average puts Talarico up by 1.2 percentage points, 46 percent to Paxton’s 44.8 percent. Polls go back and forth on who leads in the Lone Star state, often with statistical leads within the margin of error. Kansas Senate Race Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has emerged as one of the party's strongest fundraisers in Kansas in recent years, but the path to unseating Republican Senator Roger Marshall remains difficult in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly a century. Since then, Republicans have maintained an uninterrupted hold on both of the state's Senate seats. The streak is among the longest active Republican runs in the country. Fox News shifted the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican," a rating that still favors the GOP but suggests Democrats have made gains in what has traditionally been a reliably Republican contest. After Reverend Adam Hamilton secured the Democratic nomination in August, The Cook Political Report moved the Kansas Senate race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican.” "A Democratic breakthrough in Kansas is a longshot," Klink told Newsweek in an email Tuesday. He continued, "Adam Hamilton, a well-known minister, raised nearly $3.7 million in his first two months and cleared an eleven-candidate primary. That said, Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Senator Marshall enters the fall with unified GOP support behind him." Public polling in the race has been limited, and several of the surveys conducted so far were commissioned by Democratic groups. A Democratic-sponsored Public Policy Polling survey of 569 Kansas voters found Marshall with a one percentage point lead, 46 percent to Hamilton’s 45 percent, with about 9 percent undecided. That poll was conducted between August 7 and 8. A January poll by Tavern Research found Marshall leading Hamilton by 8 percentage points, 54 percent to 46 percent. The poll of 1,013 likely voters was conducted between January 26-28, and has a margin of error of ±4 percentage points. Other forecasting models and polling aggregators continue to rate the race as leaning Republican. Marshall won his 2020 Senate race by roughly 11 points, and Republicans have consistently carried Kansas in presidential elections by double-digit margins. Trump won the state by more than 16 percentage points in 2024, underscoring the GOP's strength at the federal level. Michigan Senate Race Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed will go against Republican Mike Rogers for the open Senate seat following Democrat Gary Peters' decision to retire. Democrats have held the seat for decades. The state backed Trump in two of the past three presidential elections, but Democrats have continued to notch major statewide victories, emphasizing Michigan's status as one of the nation's most closely divided battlegrounds. Michigan has long defied easy political labels, often producing razor-thin elections and unexpected outcomes. In 2016, Democratic primary voters backed independent Vermont Senator Sanders over Hillary Clinton before narrowly helping deliver the state to Trump months later. Since then, Michigan has alternated between Democratic and Republican presidential support, cementing its battleground status. Many of the races have been close. Trump won the state in 2024 with 49.7 percent to Vice President Kamala Harris’ 48.3 percent. In 2020, President Joe Biden won the state over Trump, 50.6 percent to 47.8 percent. Trump narrowly secured the state in his first campaign in 2016, beating Clinton by about .20 percent. Fox News polling shows Rogers flipping the seat, and the forecast changed from “likely Democrat” to “toss up.” The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball also rate the race as a toss-up. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Michigan voters found Rogers ahead at 51 percent to El-Sayed’s 47 percent, with 2 percent undecided. The poll, which was conducted August 6-10, had a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. A survey from Michigan pollster EPIC-MRA showed Rogers up 3 percent over El-Sayed with 46 percent compared to 43 percent. The poll was taken before the primary election from July 24 to July 31 among 600 respondents and had a margin of error of ±4 percent. A Mitchell Research & Communications poll also taken before the primary showed a tie, with both candidates landing at 45 percent. news.title: AP Interview: Ralph Norman questions Trump's endorsement of Darline Graham in South Carolina runoff
news.text:
ANDERSON, S.C. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman says it’s a “head scratcher” that President Donald Trump endorsed Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Republican Senate runoff, saying his experience in Congress and business — and consistent votes for Trump’s priorities — make him the stronger candidate to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Norman’s comments came in a wide-ranging interview with The Associated Press ahead of the Aug. 25 GOP runoff to pick a replacement for the senator, who died unexpectedly last month. In a state that routinely elects only Republicans for statewide office, GOP primaries are often the most contentious competitions. Tuesday’s winner will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November.

Norman finished second to Graham in a 10-candidate special primary on Aug. 11, though neither won the majority needed to win outright. AP’s request for a similar interview with Graham has not been granted.

Darline Graham was appointed as interim senator after her brother’s death. She opted to run in the special primary for a full term, something she said Trump — long an ally of her brother — urged her to do. Darline Graham says she’s accomplished much during her time as interim, has years of experience running a state agency in South Carolina and will continue to advocate for Trump’s goals in the Senate.

Norman said he’s skeptical that South Carolina voters have had enough time to vet the political newcomer for a six-year term, while he’s already been through a statewide campaign this cycle, coming up short in the June gubernatorial primary. He also eschewed the millions being spent on ads against him, much of it from a super PAC that had been aligned with Lindsey Graham and now supports Darline Graham.

Norman backed former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary, but has since been a Trump supporter.

Here are excerpts from the AP’s conversation with Norman about the race. This transcript has been edited for space and clarity:

You oppose ‘endless wars’ and support Trump. What should the U.S. do next on Iran?

A: If you read the mood of the public across the country, it’s, “we want gas prices down.” They don’t understand what’s left.

(Trump) did a great job of taking out the nuclear threat that we had for 40 years. … but there’s still a lot of work to be done. The American people do not understand the Strait of Hormuz not being completely controlled by America. That’s what I hear. And gas prices, as a result, are staying high. And I think one of the worst things the president wants is the public to turn on him because he’s not ending it.

Now, what does ending it mean? Well, no one really knows. I mean, does it mean, just a remnant of leaders that are opposed to him? Does it mean bombing? He mentioned that he was going to take out the electrical supplies. He was going to decimate the country. Well, that hasn’t happened. So, I think it’s a communication issue that he needs to get involved with.

So I think he’d be doing himself a big favor to explain more now. He says it’s under no timeline. Well, when the public turns on you, they turn on you.

How does Trump’s support for Graham complicate your campaign?

A: Imagine if I went to (head football coach) Dabo Swinney at Clemson and any of the coaches and said: “Look, I got a prospect I want you to look at, and I want them to. They can start. I want you to sign them up. They can start for the next six years.” “What’s the qualifications?” “They’re kin to Tom Brady.” Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here.

It’s politics. It’s votes, and I’ve stuck with it, and I will continue to.

Has Darline Graham done enough to let voters get to know her?

A: It’s not the fact that she hasn’t been in politics. Now, she’s worked at a governmental agency. I’ve run a business. I’ve made money and I’ve lost money, and that’s the drawback for any politician. You need to have done that. I have demonstrated that I want to get the national debt solved, which is the cancer that I see is bankrupting this country, but by dodging debates, that’s going to hurt her, and it should.

You got to get out there and answer all questions.

She can run a campaign like she wants to. What’s happened? She’s told the Washington elite they’re dictating the terms because it’s not South Carolina money. Mine is my money and South Carolina’s money, so they’re dictating the terms and giving her the political answers, like Biden: Don’t show up, be in a basement. His was because he was senile. Hers is they want her to win this election.

The powers that be do not want Ralph Norman in there, and it would be questioned, what’s the return on investment that they’re having to come after me like that? What’s the return on investment for the president? If I were your typical politician, I would say, “No, that makes me mad, I’m gonna stop him at every level.” I’m not gonna do that. I don’t play like that. It would be horrible if Kamala Harris had won this. He saved the country, and I really think that. He should go on Rushmore. He really should. What he’s done, it took guts.

But this one is a head scratcher. I’m gonna win this election. We’re gonna win this election, and unless something happens that I, you know — I can just feel it. People are with us, and I’ve got a record they can’t dispute.

Does support from Nikki Haley hurt you in a race dominated by Trump?

A: No. And I told the president it was a loyalty issue. I came in with Nikki. She’s from South Carolina, and he understands that. And again, anybody can take anything and use it to say that was a reason. Look, the minute she lost (the 2024 presidential primary against Trump), I called him, and my record since he’s been in office has been lock solid.

It’s because I believe in him. I just believe what he’s doing. Now I don’t like what he’s doing now, but he’s president. I give him all the leeway to do it if that’s what you want to do. But he’s done so many good things, right, to me.

Voters have to decide that. I mean, if they want to hold that against me, it’s out there. I’m not apologizing.

If elected, what would be your Senate priorities?

A: People bait us, “Are you gonna fire (Senate Majority Leader John) Thune?” Well, it’s deeper than that. One, I wouldn’t do it to somebody that I wouldn’t have a conversation with first. When you fire anybody, you talk with them, and you come to an agreement. You either disagree or agree. I would get with Thune, who is a nice man, from what I’ve been hearing, say, “How can we work on getting the SAVE Act passed? Now, if it’s still the same, “We don’t have the votes. We’re not going to try anything,” and then I’ll just say, “Well, fine, I’m going to work to replace you, and we’ll see who that is.”

Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

news.title: David Crowley's Chances of Beating Tom Tiffany: First Post-Primary Poll
news.text: Democrat David Crowley held a narrow lead over Republican Tom Tiffany in the first poll of the Wisconsin governor race released since the two candidates won their primaries earlier in August. Wisconsin’s gubernatorial contest is poised to be one of the most competitive of the 2026 midterm elections. Incumbent Governor Tony Evers, a Democrat, is retiring at the end of his term, leaving open a seat in one of the most closely divided swing states. Tiffany, a congressman backed by President Donald Trump, easily won the GOP nomination—but Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, narrowly eked out a victory over democratic socialist state Representative Francesca Hong in the Democratic primary. David Crowley Leads New Wisconsin Poll The new poll from Platform Communications, first reported by Wisconsin Public Radio, showed Crowley up 4 points over Tiffany, 48 percent to 44 percent. Wisconsin voters viewed Crowley more favorably, with a +17 net favorability rating: 43 percent viewed him positively and 26 percent negatively. Tiffany’s favorability sat at -5 points, with 38 percent viewing him favorably and 43 percent unfavorably. The poll surveyed 500 likely voters from August 12-13, 2026. The race is competitive, but Crowley has a slight advantage, Henrik Schatzinger, a professor of political science at Ripon College, told Newsweek on Tuesday. He said four points is a “lead” but “not a cushion.” “Wisconsin is still closely divided, but Democrats have performed well in recent statewide races. Crowley starts the general election in a solid position,” Schatzinger said. He said Democrats have handled the aftermath of the primary “quite well.” “The Democratic primary was a roller coaster, but the general election began with something closer to a group hug. Now the question is whether Democrats can turn that hug into turnout. Hong has already helped Crowley build the bridge back to progressives. The question is whether her voters cross it in November,” he said. Tiffany responded to the poll in a statement to Newsweek, writing that he is “focused on lowering taxes, cutting costs, and letting Wisconsin families keep more of their hard-earned money.” “David Crowley nearly doubled Milwaukee County’s sales tax, raised property taxes, and oversaw spending that has left the county facing massive deficits. The more voters see his record, the clearer the choice becomes: he failed Milwaukee County, and we cannot let him fail Wisconsin,” he said. Crowley, meanwhile, said in a statement that Wisconsin voters “agree that Congressman Tom Tiffany and his MAGA agenda are too extreme for the Badger State.” “That’s why working families across Wisconsin are joining our movement to defeat Congressman Tiffany, who has spent nearly 20 years as a career politician trying to push our state backwards. We will continue meeting folks in every corner of the state and talk about how I will lower costs, fund our public schools, and build a brighter future for our kids and grandkids as the next governor of Wisconsin,” he wrote. What Do Other Polls and Prediction Markets Show? The new poll aligns with earlier surveys showing Crowley with a modest lead over Tiffany. A GBAO poll, which surveyed 800 likely voters from July 30 to August 3 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points, showed Crowley up 3 points over Tiffany, 47 percent to 44 percent. A separate poll from RMG Research and the Napolitan News Service showed Crowley up 3 points, 46 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 800 registered voters from July 20-24, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Crowley is favored in prediction markets, having a 75 percent chance of winning on Kalshi and a 78 percent chance on Polymarket as of Tuesday morning. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment in the moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Data Centers Become Focus in Wisconsin A major issue in Wisconsin’s governor race is data centers, and Crowley is facing GOP attacks over his stance on the issue. Crowley told NBC News after his victory that he does not believe a moratorium on data centers would work in Wisconsin. Schatzinger said data centers may be Crowley’s “clearest vulnerability.” “Public opinion in Wisconsin has moved sharply against data centers, and Crowley's earlier comments about Wisconsin becoming a national or global hub give Republicans something very concrete to use against him. Crowley’s problem is that Republicans don’t have to explain his position on data centers. Tiffany can simply play the clip of him talking about Wisconsin becoming a national and global data-center hub, and he is already doing it,” he said. Tiffany’s campaign released an attack ad against Crowley for his position on data centers, calling him “Data Center David Crowley,” highlighting his comments that Wisconsin could become a hub for AI and attacking him for supporting a tax incentive for data centers. Crowley, meanwhile, has outlined his own plan on data centers. His campaign website says he would “let communities decide for themselves” whether they want to construct a data center. He also called for guardrails, including requiring 100 percent renewable energy, covering 100 percent of the costs of infrastructure and grid updates, and banning NDAs. Tiffany previously voiced positive views on data centers in February, calling them an “exciting new technology,” but said ratepayers should not be harmed. “It would be unfair to existing manufacturers, for them to pay much higher electricity rates just because a new industry came in. So we’re going to probably have to find a new template if AI and the data centers specifically come into Wisconsin,” he said, according to PBS Wisconsin. In the primary, Hong drew national attention for calling for a moratorium on new data centers. David Crowley Pulled Off Shock Primary Victory Over Francesca Hong In the primary, Hong had carved out a substantial lead in the polls over Crowley, who exited from the race earlier in the summer but reentered amid concerns about Hong’s electability in the general election by some in the Democratic establishment. He narrowly won by less than half a percentage point. His surge came after polling showing Hong trailing Tiffany in the general election resurfaced social media posts that drew negative attention to her campaign and raised anxiety among some Democrats. In 2020, Hong said on Twitter: "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621." She has since backtracked, saying recently: "I'm not going to cancel Thanksgiving," and "I will be celebrating Thanksgiving with my family this year." Hong also struggled to win over endorsements from prominent progressives like New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders. Some prominent Democrats worried about Hong’s chances in a general election, worrying that past remarks like that and her identification as a democratic socialist could alienate moderate, independent voters in the state. “The Dem race for governor in WI feels like a slow-rolling car headed for a cliff. If Dems there don't figure it out, they'll endanger a potential House pickup opportunity and risk installing as governor an election-denying, Freedom Caucus member just in time for the '28 election,” Democratic strategist David Axelrod wrote in a July 23 post on X. Wisconsin Is Key Swing State Wisconsin is one of the nation's most competitive states. In 2024, Trump won 49.6 percent of the vote compared to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 48.7 percent. In 2020, former President Joe Biden won the state with 49.5 percent of the vote to Trump’s 48.8 percent, flipping the state after Trump won it in 2016. That year, Trump received 47.2 percent of the vote compared to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s 46.5 percent. The state's political geography has shifted significantly in recent years. Republicans have consolidated strength among rural, white working-class voters, many of whom previously supported Obama. Democrats counter this by maintaining high turnout in urban centers like Milwaukee and Madison, alongside growing margins in affluent suburban areas. Wisconsin last elected a Republican governor in 2014, when former Governor Scott Walker won reelection. He lost reelection to Evers four years later in 2018. What Happens Next The Cook Political Report views the race as a toss-up, while Sabato’s Crystal Ball gives Crowley an advantage, rating the race as Leans Democratic. Crowley and Tiffany will spend the coming months making their cases to voters to win in the deeply competitive state. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Crowley led a new poll of Wisconsin after his victory in the contentious primary against Francesca Hong.
