news.title: Think urban and rural Missouri is divided? Amendment 4 said otherwise | Opinion
news.text:
Two weeks ago, the voters in two Missouri counties that took diametrically opposed positions in the 2024 presidential election went to the polls — and tied for the second-highest percentage of votes against Amendment 4.

Amendment 4, as you may recall, was proposed by the state legislature and would have made passing citizen-led ballot measures significantly harder. No longer would a simple statewide majority suffice. Instead, these questions would have to win a majority of votes in every single one of Missouri’s eight congressional districts.

Missourians have used the citizen petition process to go around the General Assembly (more specifically, the Republican supermajority within it) to legalize marijuana, expand Medicaid, increase the minimum wage, require employers to provide earned sick leave for employees and protect abortion rights. If the new threshold as proposed by Amendment 4 had been in place when these petition issues were on the ballot, none of them would have passed.

On Aug. 4, Missourians went to the polls to vote on this new, more stringent standard — and soundly rejected it in every county across the state. Statewide, 80% of Missourians voted against it.

Looking at The New York Times’ county-by-county vote percentages piqued my interest. St. Louis had the highest percentage of no votes, which likely surprises no one.

But two very different counties tied for second place, with 86% of voters in each rejecting the measure.

The first county was Jackson County — the state’s second-largest by population. Urban and diverse, Kamala Harris carried Jackson County by 19 points in 2024.

The second was Grundy County, a mostly rural county in the north-center of the state that is home to less than 10,000 people. Just under 1 in 4 Grundy County residents is over 65 —– compared to roughly 1 in 6 in Jackson County. Ninety-three percent of Grundy County residents are white, and 17% percent have a bachelor’s degree. Just 77% have broadband internet.

And Donald Trump carried Grundy County by 64 points in 2024.

If you were to envision those two counties, you would probably put them on the opposite ends of the spectrum. They do not share a geographic region, demographics or presidential preferences.

But that didn’t matter on Aug. 4.

I co-founded and run an organization that funds Democratic state legislative candidates in some of the reddest districts in the country, including in Missouri. In that work, I spend a lot of time talking to Democrats who are running in places such as Grundy County.

They tell me stories about talking to Republican voters who leave the conversation heartened that someone is willing to listen to them, and shocked by how much they agree.

Ask people in any county what’s actually squeezing them and you’ll probably hear the same list. Prices are too high and wages are too low. Health insurance is hard to get and doesn’t cover enough. Healthcare is expensive and hard to find. They’ll talk about school funding and how they’re worried about their kids’ (or grandkids’) education. And they might even mention that they’re frustrated with a state legislature that seems more interested in stoking divisions than conquering the problems that we face.

None of those problems starts or stops at county lines.

The suggestion that “urban” and “rural” America agree on nothing and are basically different countries sharing a state government gets a lot of air time on cable news and social media, where conflict drives views. Sadly, it’s also furthered by some politicians — maybe because a divided electorate is easier to manipulate than a united one.

But the reality is not so simple.

The people drawing the battle lines between city and country in Missouri have a lot riding on all of us believing those lines are real and fixed. They’re not.

Missouri voters proved that on Aug. 4.

Michele Hornish is co-founder and executive director of the political action committee Every State Blue.

news.title: South Carolina’s move to front of 2028 Democratic primary calendar could benefit Kamala Harris
news.text:
Harris first teased another White House bid in front of a predominantly African American crowd at Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network convention in April.

 “I am thinking about it,” she told Sharpton.

Harris is likely to face stiff competition for the 2028 Democratic nomination, including possibly from several high-profile Black Democrats. Gov. Wes Moore (D-MD) and Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ), in particular, are both seen as potential presidential candidates. Unlike Harris, the duo also lacks the baggage of having served in the Biden administration.

“Both of those candidates would really have to build up some sort of momentum that just is not there for them right now,” Shroff said about the two possible contenders. “Kamala Harris has already built a national campaign, yes, in a shortened timeline. But Wes Moore has, for example, been insisting he’s not running. And by the way, I don’t know that it’s his time to do so. He doesn’t have that impressive a record to run on.”

Members of the Democratic National Committee officially approved South Carolina to vote first in 2028 over Iowa and New Hampshire, which have traditionally kicked off the nominating contest, over the weekend as part of the Democratic Party’s desire to prioritize diversity in the early voting states.

Black voters are among the Democratic Party’s most loyal voting blocs. After the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais decision enabled southern states to eliminate several majority-minority districts, DNC members claimed it was pivotal that South Carolina vote first.

“South Carolina’s earned every right to go first,” said veteran Democratic strategist James Carville. “I think that it is a recognition on the part of the Democratic Party that blacks are essential to our coalition, probably the most loyal part of the coalition, and I’m glad to see that they have a fairly prominent position. It would have been a shame if we’d done anything else.”

But South Carolina’s black electorate is not monolithic, and Harris could face challenges among both younger voters and those looking for a break from the Biden era.

“If Gov. Moore is in the race, he’s an African American male and is more of a generational change a little bit … because he’s much younger than her, would he also garner enough votes to overtake her?” said Douglas Wilson, who also served as a regional field director in South Carolina during former President Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign. “As far as progressives go, that still remains to be seen because a lot of the progressive Left were not really big Kamala fans during the campaign because of the stance in Gaza.”

Some black voters previously told the Washington Examiner they were hesitant to vote for Harris after two Democratic women have lost to President Donald Trump. But Wilson said Harris’s most pressing issue is that she represents the Biden administration, and the party appears to want new leadership.

The Biden-Harris administration’s support of Israel in its battle against Hamas became a significant source of friction between Harris and younger progressive voters during the 2024 campaign.

Another major variable is Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-SC), whose endorsement helped Biden consolidate support among the state’s black voters ahead of his decisive 2020 victory. Any 2028 contender will likely seek the support of Clyburn and the political network surrounding him.

“When you look at the breakdown of the black voters there, it’s still relatively middle-aged to older voters,” Wilson said. “And that’s how Joe Biden was able to win South Carolina because a lot of those voters are still endeared and tied to Clyburn and listen to him.”

DNC APPROVES 2028 PRIMARY SCHEDULE, GIVES SOUTH CAROLINA THE FIRST SPOT

Michael Ceraso, a Democratic strategist who worked on Buttigieg’s presidential campaign, cautioned against oversimplifying the Palmetto State’s African American voters.

“I think it’d be foolish for any operative or consultant or any narrator to say that like Harris can or cannot win South Carolina this early on,” he said. “But I think it’s good to look at her past and how she’s run for office before and take an assessment on that and … what would she do. And I think the past is always a good indicator [of] what someone is gonna do in the present.”

Naomi Lim contributed to this report.

news.title: Democrats’ South Carolina presidential-primary scheme is a last-ditch effort to hold off the DSA
news.text:
Don’t believe the Democratic National Committee’s official storyline: The DNC’s decision to make South Carolina the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028 isn’t about introducing more racial diversity into the early contests.

It’s actually about keeping power in the hands of the party establishment — the people who backed Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Joe Biden in 2020, and who are likely to wind up supporting Kamala Harris in 2028.

The fix is in.

South Carolina was the establishment’s firewall against Bernie Sanders’ left-wing insurgency twice over. 

In 2016, Sanders nearly beat Hillary Clinton in the first caucus, in Iowa, and went on to defeat her in the New Hampshire primary.

Four years later, there was a brief moment when Sanders looked like the frontrunner — until he got clobbered by Joe Biden in South Carolina.

It’s true that the black voters who make South Carolina’s primaries more racially diverse than the contests in Iowa or New Hampshire are also less politically radical.

So it’s easy for the DNC to say it’s not trying to choke off support for the socialist wing of the party; it’s just giving black voters more of a say.

The Democratic Socialists of America, the left fringe of the party, is disproportionately white — even its New York City chapter is 60% white, according to DSA’s own membership polling.

That’s astonishing, considering NYC itself is only 34% white.

This racial split between the Democrats’ most ideologically intense faction and the party’s elite, which only holds on to power thanks to black voters’ loyalty, is a fault line with the potential to reshape American politics.

South Carolina doesn’t just lean toward establishment Democrats, it backs them overwhelmingly — nearly three-quarters of the state’s Dem primary voters chose Clinton over Sanders in ’16, while Biden beat Sanders there in ’20 by a ratio of more than two-to-one.

A candidate like Harris or her fellow Californian Gavin Newsom fits that profile, and Harris’ unbeatable name recognition — as a former VP and 2024 nominee — and race-and-sex diversity qualifications likely give her an edge.

DSA members won’t stay home and let another Republican succeed Donald Trump, rather than turn out to vote for Harris or Newsom — but if the establishment candidate goes on to lose in November ’28, the party will be ripe for a revolution.

Will black voters who have so far resisted Sanders-style socialism be just as content with a DSA-led party as they have been with the Democrats’ old guard?

Meanwhile, with Republican states growing while blue states like California shed population and businesses, the Democrats face a terminal problem in the Electoral College and in the US House of Representatives. 

With each decennial census, Republicans stand to gain House seats and electoral votes.

But Democrats can offset the GOP’s growth advantages if they start flipping southern states back into the blue column.

Georgia is the test case: The state has prospered under Republican leadership, but that prosperity has fueled the growth of Atlanta, and has turned many of the city’s suburbs blue.

Virginia, of course, has already become a purple state, if not a reliably Democratic one.

And while Washington, DC, is a unique influence as the center of the federal government, the growth of the Old Dominion’s deep-blue DC suburbs — which keep extending further into Virginia’s interior — is not so different from the effect Atlanta is having on Georgia.

North Carolina is another weak link in the Republican Party’s southern wall.

So despite backing recent losers — Hillary Clinton a decade ago, Biden and Harris both in the last election — the Democratic establishment thinks it’s hit upon a strategy both for keeping control of the party and wresting the South away from Republicans. 

And it’s confident the DSA will fall in with the party line: After all, the elite Democrats are more allergic to the socialist label than they are to socialistic policies. 

They can give DSA much of what it wants. 

Yet a plan is one thing — the reality is there’s a knife fight for control of the Democratic Party, and these pieces won’t fit together easily. 

And while the Democrats’ emerging opportunities are in the South, the party’s ideologically ascendant faction is the least suited to capitalize on them.

That gives Republicans a chance to stop both the Democrats’ socialism and their racial spoils system.

To do it the GOP will have to campaign for the South like it’s a battleground region — and slow, even if it can’t immediately reverse, the drift of America’s cities to the left.

Republicans need the South and the Rust Belt — the combination that led to victory in 2016 and 2024.

If the GOP can’t compete in cities, even those in flourishing red states, the party is on the road to extinction.

Daniel McCarthy is the editor of Modern Age: A Conservative Review.

news.title: Florida primaries put unlikely candidates on Tuesday’s ballot
news.text:
In the race to replace Rep. Byron Donalds, three candidates carry records that would once have threatened to end a campaign: a pardoned felon, a one-term congressman driven from his seat in another state and a man once imprisoned for his role in Jan. 6. In the governor's race, Donalds himself is fending off a far-right challenger who has run a racist campaign, while Democrats are poised to nominate a former Republican congressman. And in a South Florida House seat, a Democratic congressman is being challenged from the left by a democratic socialist.

All of them are on the ballot Tuesday in a state where primary divisions are testing what it means to be either a Democrat or a Republican in a state that not so long ago was closely divided but is now reliably red. 

Donalds is favored to win the Republican primary in his race, a major step toward becoming the first Black Republican governor in the United States since the Reconstruction Era — provided he overcomes a field of challengers that includes a far-right candidate who has run an openly racist campaign against him. He has President Donald Trump’s endorsement. He does not have Gov. Ron DeSantis’s: The term-limited governor has stayed out of the race to succeed him — a field that also includes his lieutenant governor, a former speaker of the state House and James Fishback, who has posted on social media calling Donalds “a SLAVE” who “only wants to please his corporate masters.” 

Donalds has largely declined to engage those provocations, running instead against the opposition he expects in November.

“If we do not make sure that we keep Florida red, the democrat socialists will have a field day ripping down everything that Ron DeSantis has done to lead Florida to number one in all of this country,” Donalds said at a recent campaign event. 

He has risen quickly in Republican politics. After winning a first congressional term in 2020, he was among the House Republicans who objected to certifying Biden’s victories in two key states even after the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol and, two years later, earned votes from colleagues in the speaker of the House race after Republicans regained control of the chamber and struggled to side with a leader. 

The race to replace Donalds in Congress however is among the oddest this cycle. Former Rep. Chris Collins, who represented a New York district before being sentenced to prison as part of an insider trading case, is running after being pardoned by Trump during the final days of the president’s first term. Other contenders in the race include former North Carolina Rep. Madison Cawthorn, who lost his old seat in a 2022 primary after a single alienating term, and John Strand, who spent time imprisoned after he took part in the Jan. 6 riot. Other candidates are also running on the Republican side, including one with Trump’s support. 

Incumbents are facing challenges of their own as well. Heading into Tuesday, a dozen members of Congress have been defeated in primaries this year around the country. Rep. Cory Mills could be next: The Florida Republican is running for another term amid allegations of misconduct, and two of his colleagues in the state’s U.S. House delegation are instead backing Ryan Elijah, a former local television anchor, to be the GOP pick in the district. 

The map itself has also scrambled recent decision making for voters. Under the district lines used in 2024, Democrats won eight districts in Florida and Republicans won 20. A redraw this spring pushed by DeSantis could cut the Democrats down to holding just four seats — a shift that has improved GOP chances of keeping a narrow hold on the U.S. House this fall and has created a crunch for Democrats and driven rifts on the left. 

One race Democrats are keen on is the redrawn seat Rep. Jared Moskowitz is trying to win and keep away from Republicans. He is being challenged from the left in Tuesday’s primary by Oliver Larkin, who is being boosted by the Democratic Socialists of America.

Even after a series of DSA primary victories in blue parts of the country in recent weeks, a democratic socialist defeating Moskowitz in a district Democrats are counting on as they hope to win back the House would be one of most unlikely, and improbable, upsets of the summer, and potentially end up helping Republicans this fall. 

“There’s a rejection of this kind of status quo politics, because we went back to President Biden, and the change that we were expecting to see was not fully delivered.” Larkin told MS NOW in a late June interview. 

To try and lead the state as governor, the left is likely to nominate someone who has spent time beating Democrats, and even being defeated by the party: former Rep. David Jolly, who had a stint in Congress as a Republican until he lost a 2016 election. 

“I fought the Tea Party and lost. I fought the Freedom Caucus and lost. I fought Trumpism and lost,” Jolly said. “...I'm a proud Florida Democrat, not a reluctant one, but I'm not running to save the Democratic Party. I'm not. I'm running to be governor of Florida. And when we prove that we're worthy of people's trust, that we can govern, then we grow the Democratic Party.”

Not so long ago, Florida was a competitive political state. But after a narrow victory in 2018 to win his first term as governor, DeSantis easily won a second term in 2022. 

While Florida was still contested by eventual President Joe Biden and the Democratic Party in 2020, where their loss was in the low single digits, in 2024 Vice President Kamala Harris lost the state by 13 points. And races for Senate after 2018 in the state have been easy wins for the GOP, solidifying its shift from a competitive target to one where Democrats are struggling. 

Yet midterms tend to punish the president's party. Democrats are relying on that to help in a state where little else has gone their way lately.

Laura Haefeli contributed reporting to this article.

news.title: Stephen A. Smith Warns NABJ Will ‘Regret’ Giving Him ‘Thumbs Down’ Award: ‘They’ve Made Me More Intense’

news.title: Stephen A. Smith calls 'Thumbs Down' award by Black journalist group a 'hit job'
news.text: Stephen A. Smith fired back at the National Assn. of Black Journalists on Monday, calling its decision to give him a "Thumbs Down" award, because of his consistent criticism of Black female politicians, a political and "personal hit job." In a 44-minute address on his YouTube channel, the outspoken sports commentator said that while he was "far from perfect and ... will always try to do better on behalf of my community and for the journalism community and beyond, that does not negate the bulls— that the NABJ did." He added, "I've received a lot of insults in my day, but that might be the lowest." Smith said the award, which was given Saturday at the organization's gala, had nothing to do with journalism, attributing the dishonor to board members unhappy with his political opinions. "They did not engage in journalism when it came to critiquing me," he said. "People are scared," he added, calling himself a registered independent. "See, I talk too much and I don't speak glowingly enough about the Democratic party." He called out NABJ President Errin Haines, who is editor-at-large for the nonprofit news outlet the 19th, saying she and other board members did not reach out. "What you did to me was beneath the organization," Smith said. He said he invited Haines to discuss the award on the air but she declined, saying she would prefer a private conversation off the air. The NABJ pushed back on Smith's account of the conversation. "President Haines welcomed the opportunity to speak with Mr. Smith and proposed that they begin with a private conversation focused on listening, accountability and meaningful dialogue, with the opportunity for public engagement to follow," it said Monday in a statement. "At no point did President Haines decline a conversation with Mr. Smith or rule out a future public conversation." Other recipients of the "Thumbs Down" award included Brendan Carr, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission; DuJuan McCoy, Circle City Broadcasting president and chief executive; CBS News and the Washington Post. The statement continued: "As President Haines emphasized in her remarks Saturday night, the purpose of the Thumbs Down Award is not permanent condemnation or criticism for criticism’s sake. Accountability should create an opportunity for reflection, dialogue and progress. NABJ remains open to meaningful engagement with any of this year’s recipients and will continue fulfilling its responsibility to advocate for Black journalists, fair and accurate coverage of Black communities, and a strong and independent press." In its presentation of the award, the NABJ said Smith "has established a recurring public pattern of disparaging commentary directed at prominent Black women across politics, sports and media." The statement continued, "Such commentary reinforces harmful narratives, undermines the fair and respectful representation of Black women in public discourse and stands in direct conflict with NABJ's longstanding commitment to accurate, responsible and inclusive portrayals of Black communities." Smith then took to social media vowing he would strike back: "This is the epitome of Christmas arriving early. The NABJ wants to call folks out, fine! You had your turn, now mine is coming. And make no mistake…..,I’m coming," he wrote. Smith has been increasingly vocal about his politics as he hints at a possible presidential run. His statements, bombastic delivery and occasional praise for President Trump have come under fire in Black media and with celebrities. He accused Democratic Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas last September of using “street verbiage” in her frequent criticisms of Trump. He also has been critical of former First Lady Michelle Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, tennis star Serena Williams and others. Smith defended those remarks Monday, saying he felt he was being fair and was supportive of the women. He declared that supporting Black women always has been a priority in his life. "Everything I am, everything that I have achieved, everything that has lifted me up in my life has been associated with Black women. They have been my strength, my source of inspiration and so much more my entire life," he said. He added that he would not have been targeted by the Black media if he made the same sort of comments about conservative figures. During his speech, he noted how the "Thumbs Down" award marked a reversal of NABJ's previous embrace of him and his ESPN show "First Take," when it hosted live broadcasts of the program during its 2024 and 2025 conventions. Smith also implied that instead of being hammered by the NABJ, he should be celebrated because he is about to be inducted into the Broadcasting+Cable Hall of Fame. The NABJ statement further outlined the history of the "Thumbs Down" award, saying it has been handed out 44 times since it was first presented in 1989. The designation holds "individuals and institutions across the media landscape accountable when their reporting, commentary or practices have conflicted with the organization’s mission and values. Recipients over the years have included Black and non-Black individuals and institutions. NABJ calls balls and strikes based on the conduct and issues before us, not the identity of the recipient." Despite his anger, Smith told listeners he had no ill will toward the organization. "Please continue to support the NABJ," he said.
news.summary: In a video posted on his YouTube channel Monday, the ESPN sports commentator called the 'Thumbs Down' award given by the National Assn. of Black Journalists 'beneath the organization.'

news.title: Want to 233x your money? Why this new form of gambling is a dangerous trap
news.text:
It is illegal for these prediction market providers to operate in Australia; however, it takes as little as a $10 VPN to join them. Even worse, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) – the regulator that ordered the ban – admits that using a VPN to circumvent geo-blockers is completely legal.

They aren’t all bad news. According to Australian-American economist Professor Justin Wolfers, “prediction markets produce better forecasts than the alternative, whether that’s polls, pundits, models, or other approaches”.

Prediction markets are comprised of a few sophisticated bettors against masses of small gamblers who guess based on little more than vibes.

In the 2024 US presidential election, for example, opinion polls narrowly favoured Kamala Harris, while prediction markets had Donald Trump as the clear favourite. Trump went on to win every swing state. But why does this matter?

Better predictions allow people, businesses and governments to make better decisions about the future. Wolfers argues that having “high-quality forecasts of the likelihood of the Strait of Hormuz opening”, for example, would be of great value to businesses.
news.summary: If Australia is serious about keeping prediction markets out, the existing ban needs teeth, and the government needs to step up and act.

news.title: What to expect in CA's special congressional election to fill Eric Swalwell's seat
news.text:
Four months after Democratic U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell resigned from Congress amid sexual assault allegations that torpedoed his campaign for California governor, his former Bay Area constituents will pick a replacement Tuesday to serve out the rest of his term.

With two Democrats competing on the ballot, the seat in California's 14th Congressional District is guaranteed to remain under Democratic control and further narrow an already fragile Republican majority in the chamber.

RELATED: Rep. Eric Swalwell resigns from Congress after sexual assault allegations

State Sen. Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Board President Melissa Hernandez were the finalists in the June 16 special primary, in which the top two finishers regardless of party affiliation advanced to Tuesday's special election. The two also will compete in the fall in a slightly redrawn district for a full term that begins in January 2027.

Wahab placed first in both the June 16 special primary and the June 2 primary for the full-term seat to replace Swalwell, who has denied the allegations against him. In both contests, Wahab led Hernandez by more than 20 percentage points.

Hernandez has more than doubled Wahab's fundraising and spending for the campaign, but as of the end of July the two were on roughly even footing in terms of cash in the bank.

The race has also attracted the attention of several outside groups, including some affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a powerful pro-Israel lobbying organization. United Democracy Project, a super political action committee backed by AIPAC, spent $1.2 million on the race in August in support of Hernandez and in opposition to Wahab, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Another group, Bold America, which has received funding from United Democracy Project, has spent about $1.7 million on the race since the special primary, also in support of Hernandez and in opposition to Wahab.

RELATED: East Bay congressional race to replace Eric Swalwell heats up between Aisha Wahab, Melissa Hernandez

Collectively, outside groups have spent about $4.1 million on the race since mid-July. About $3.7 million was spent to benefit Hernandez's campaign, compared with just shy of $400,000 to benefit Wahab's.

The boundaries of the 14th Congressional District were redrawn as part of a new congressional map approved by voters in a 2025 statewide ballot measure known as Proposition 50. The map goes into effect for the full-term seat in January, while the winner of the special election will serve under the current boundaries for the remainder of the year.

Proposition 50 was placed on the ballot in response to mid-decade redistricting efforts led by President Donald Trump in several Republican-controlled states. While the plan created a congressional map more favorable to Democrats, no dramatic changes were made to the 14th District. Under the current boundaries, Democrats make up 50.4% of registered voters in October, compared with 17.6% for Republicans. Under the new boundaries, Democrats comprise about 49.7% of registered voters as of mid-May, compared with about 17.4% for Republicans.

In 2024, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the current 14th District with 65.8% of the vote in the presidential election against Trump. If the election had been held under the new boundaries, Harris would have received 65.4% of the vote.

Both versions of the district are contained entirely within Alameda County in the East Bay. The current district includes Hayward, Livermore, Pleasanton and Union City, as well as parts of San Leandro, Fremont and Dublin.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

Polls close at 8 p.m. PT, which is 11 p.m. ET.

What's on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the 14th Congressional District special election.

Who gets to vote?

Any registered voter in the current version of California's 14th Congressional District may participate in the special election.

How many voters are there?

As of May 2026, there were about 423,000 registered voters in the 14th Congressional District, including about 210,000 Democrats, about 73,000 Republicans and about 116,000 voters with no party preference.

How many people actually vote?

Nearly 124,000 voters cast ballots in the June 16 special primary. About 276,000 people voted in the regularly scheduled 2024 general election in the 14th District.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?

About 98% of votes in the June 16 special primary were from absentee ballots delivered in person or by mail.

As of Wednesday, about 52,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday's election, about 32,500 from Democrats, about 7,800 from Republicans and the rest from unaffiliated or third-party voters.

When are early and absentee votes released?

In Alameda County, the first vote update of the night usually includes only results from mail voting, but the county typically still has a sizable number of mail ballots left to tally by the next morning.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the June 16 special primary, the AP first reported results at 11:17 p.m. ET, or 17 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 1:03 a.m. ET, with about 87% of total votes counted. The vote count reached 99.9% complete at 7:26 p.m. ET on June 18.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it's determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

There are no automatic recounts in California. Any registered voter may request and pay for a recount. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 77 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP's coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.
news.summary: Four months after Democratic U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell resigned from Congress amid sexual assault allegations that torpedoed his campaign for California governor, his former Bay Area constituents will pick a replacement Tuesday to serve out the rest of his term.

news.title: Usha Vance’s faith tests US pluralism
news.text: p>Does the religious identity of prominent Indian Americans ever become an albatross around their neck? In Usha Vance’s case, it increasingly looks that way. The wife of Vice President J D Vance was raised Hindu and has not indicated any intention of converting to Christianity. Her faith has become a revealing fault line in American politics — one where religion, race, marriage and political power collide..Usha Vance’s Hindu identity has been discussed intensely because her husband’s political trajectory has placed their interfaith marriage under a national spotlight. Vance, a Catholic convert and one of the leading figures in the Republican Party, is widely viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 presidential nomination..In October 2025, at a Turning Point USA event in Mississippi attended by thousands, Vance was asked about his interfaith marriage and the religious upbringing of his children. He said that Usha accompanies him to church on most Sundays and that he hoped she would eventually be “moved” by the same Christian faith that had moved him. He also acknowledged that she has free will and that her not converting would not create a problem for their marriage..The episode was striking partly because of the history of their relationship. When Vance married Usha in 2014, he was not yet a Catholic; he had described himself at the time as agnostic or atheist. The couple held both Christian and Hindu wedding ceremonies, with the Hindu ceremony blessed by a Hindu priest. Five years later, in 2019, Vance converted to Catholicism..Usha, meanwhile, has accompanied him to Mass while retaining her own religious identity. Their four children are being raised in the Christian faith. The arrangement is ordinary for the compromises interfaith couples make. Yet because her husband is now vice president, the private question of religious difference has acquired a public dimension..'Obsessed with Usha': JD Vance reveals what drew him to second lady in new memoir.Vance’s memoir, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, published in June this year, has made faith even more central to his public persona. While promoting the book, Vance again defended his hope that Usha might one day share his faith, saying that when a person believes something deeply, it is natural to want loved ones to share that belief. His position may be understandable as personal conviction, but the attention reveals how little room American public life sometimes leaves for religious ambiguity..Usha is hardly a passive figure whose identity can be reduced to her husband’s politics. A Yale-trained lawyer, she clerked for Chief Justice John Roberts before joining Munger, Tolles & Olson, where she represented some of the country’s leading corporations. She has a formidable record and a mind of her own. Yet that has not shielded her from scrutiny. Nick Fuentes, the white supremacist and far-right commentator, has questioned whether a politician with an Indian wife can genuinely support “White identity”. He also mocked Vance’s decision to name his son Vivek. Vance has defended his wife against such attacks..This leaves Vance caught between two impulses within his own political coalition: one that wants his wife to become Christian, and another that regards her Indian identity as evidence that she does not belong. Usha’s predicament is not unique. Nikki Haley converted from Sikhism to Christianity before entering electoral politics. Bobby Jindal converted from Hinduism to Catholicism, and his Hindu-born wife also converted. Kamala Harris grew up with both Hindu and Black Baptist influences, reflecting the layered identity of an Indian American raised in the United States. Vivek Ramaswamy, meanwhile, has remained Hindu while building a national political profile..All these cases raise the same uncomfortable question: must the faith of a candidate—or of a candidate’s spouse—be made to resemble whatever the electorate considers familiar and acceptable?.America’s founders sought to prevent precisely such a religious qualification for public office. Article VI, Clause 3 of the US Constitution prohibits a religious test for federal office, while the First Amendment bars government from establishing religion or prohibiting its free exercise. These principles emerged from a country wary of religious establishment and coercion..The larger test is not whether Usha Vance eventually converts. It is whether she remains free not to. Her faith is hers to keep, change or reconcile in her own way. The real measure of American pluralism may be whether the country — and especially the political movement her husband leads — can accept that choice without demanding that she first become someone else..(The writer is a Delhi-based journalist).(Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of DH.)</p

news.title: Donald Trump's Approval Rating Has Crashed With Hispanic Men
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating among Hispanic and Latino men, a critical group he flipped in the 2024 election, has plummeted in recent months as his administration faces growing backlash over the economy. Hispanic and Latino voters have historically broken for Democrats, but Trump made inroads with these voters in 2024, helping propel his return to the White House in key states, especially in places like Arizona and Nevada. Democrats have worked to win back Hispanic and Latino voters in the midterms, and a key question is whether there will be a reversion back to Democrats or if those GOP gains are permanent. Winning back Hispanic and Latino men may be critical for Democrats. In 2024, Trump won Latino men by 10 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris, 54 percent to 44 percent, according to CNN exit polling data. In 2020, former President Joe Biden won Latino men by 23 points, 59 percent to 36 percent. In 2016, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points, 63 percent to 32 percent. Democrats winning back those voters could create a political challenge for Trump in the midterms in competitive states with a high Hispanic and Latino population like Texas. The shift in Hispanic and Latino polling numbers comes as Trump continues to lose ground nationwide in his approval rating. Furthermore, Republicans in states like Florida and Texas redrew their congressional maps to favor their party ahead of the midterms, largely based around the 2024 numbers. A significant reversion among Hispanic and Latino voters could lead to more of those districts becoming competitive. In a statement to Newsweek on Monday, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle wrote that November 5, 2024 was “the ultimate poll” when “nearly 80 million Americans overwhelmingly elected President Trump to deliver on his popular and commonsense agenda.” “No other President in history has accomplished more for the American people than President Trump, who is working tirelessly to create jobs, cool inflation, increase housing affordability, and more. The President has already made historic progress not only in America but around the world, and this is just the beginning as his agenda continues taking effect,” he said. Trump Approval Rating Declines with Hispanic Men CNN data analyst Harry Enten on Monday highlighted new polling data showing Trump’s approval slipping among Hispanic voters. He pointed to polling data from CNN and SSRS showing that the president’s approval rating among Hispanic men is -41 points despite winning them by 10 points less than two years ago. “All of that movement that you saw, that historic performance that President Trump had among Hispanic men, adios amigos. Goodbye. See you later,” he said. He said the shift is largely due to the economy, with data showing his approval on the economy among Hispanic men stood at -49 points, despite being more trusted by 11 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in the fall of 2024. He explained that this could have major implications for the midterms, as Hispanic men favor Democrats by 20 points in the midterms. “What we’re seeing among Hispanic men and their views of President Trump very much diving toward the negative, absolutely look like they’re going to have a massive impact on the midterm elections,” he said. That data is backed up by some other polls, though many pollsters do not release crosstab data for Hispanic men specifically, as that is often a small subset that may not always be statistically significant. Civiqs, which has surveyed more than 123,000 Americans since January 2025 on Trump’s approval rating, does provide such information. It found that 59 percent of Hispanic and Latino men disapproved of Trump, while 36 percent approved. Meanwhile, a UnidosUS poll also found him underwater with Latino men, finding his approval at 34 percent and disapproval at 64 percent. It surveyed 3,000 Latino registered voters from April 27 to May 14, 2026, and had a margin of error overall of ±1.8 percentage points. What This Means for the Midterm Elections Republicans losing ground among Hispanic voters could have major implications for the midterms. In Texas, for instance, Trump’s strong showing with Hispanic voters helped make up for a decade of Democratic gains in the state. It shifted from backing Trump by fewer than 6 points in 2020 to nearly 14 points in 2024, largely due to his support among Hispanic and Latino voters. Trump won Hispanic and Latino men by 30 points, 65 percent to 35 percent, and Hispanic voters overall by 10 points, 55 percent to 45 percent, in the Lone Star State. The Texas Senate race between Democratic state Representative James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is expected to be among the most competitive of the midterms. Building back support among Hispanic and Latino voters is critical to Talarico’s path to victory, and polling suggests he is on track to do so. A recent Emerson College poll, which found Paxton up one point overall, showed Talarico with support of 55 percent of Hispanic and Latino voters, compared to Paxton’s 36 percent support. It surveyed 1,000 likely voters from August 9 to 10, 2026 and had an overall margin of error of plus or minus ±3 percentage points. Other competitive states like Arizona and Nevada also have high percentages of Hispanic and Latino voters. Both states have competitive gubernatorial races and shifted significantly toward Trump in 2024. Arizona backed Trump by about 5.5 points, after backing Biden by less than half a percentage point in 2020. Nevada backed Biden by just over 2 points in 2020 but Trump by about 3 points in 2024. Arizona also has several competitive House races that could come down to Hispanic and Latino voters. There are also major down-ballot implications due to mid-decade redistricting. Polls showing poor approval among Hispanic voters may be especially worrying for Trump because new GOP-drawn maps in Florida and Texas were built on the assumption that Hispanic voters would continue trending toward the party as they did in 2024. If their support collapses, those redraws would become less effective—or potentially even backfire on Republicans in the Lone Star State. Republicans redrew Texas’ congressional map to make several seats in South Texas, a region with a high concentration of Hispanic voters, more conservative. It redrew seats held by Democratic Representatives Henry Cuellar of District 28, Vicente Gonzalez of District 34 and Greg Casar of District 35 to become more friendly to Republicans, but they’re not overwhelmingly conservative. If GOP support among Hispanic voters collapses, Democrats could hold onto those seats in November. That scenario could also make the more conservative seat held by Representative Monica De La Cruz of District 15 or the open seat in District 23 competitive. How Hispanic and Latino Voters Have Shifted Over the Years Overall, Trump came close to winning Latino voters in 2024, according to CNN exit polling. They backed Harris by only a 5-point margin, giving her 51 percent of the vote and Trump 46 percent. That’s a major shift from 2020 when they gave former President Joe Biden 65 percent of the vote and Trump 32 percent. Even that was a slight rightward shift from 2016, when former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won 66 percent of Latino voters, and Trump won only 28 percent. According to exit polling data from The New York Times, former President Barack Obama won Hispanic voters by a 44-point margin in 2012, 71 percent to 27 percent, and a 36-point margin in 2008, 67 percent to 31 percent. However, they were more evenly divided in 2004, when Democrat John Kerry won them by only 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Republicans can say "goodbye" to their gains among Hispanic and Latino men from 2024, CNN's data analyst Harry Enten said.

news.title: Rating changes: 10 of 11 races shift toward Democrats
news.text:
ANALYSIS — With less than three months to go before Election Day, control of both chambers of Congress remains in play. 

While Democrats lack many guaranteed pickups, there continues to be growing softness or vulnerability for Republicans on the outskirts of the House and Senate battleground. President Donald Trump’s low job approval rating is creating potential targets in red-leaning areas that aren’t typically seen as Democratic opportunities. 

One of the biggest examples is Iowa, which is competitive up and down the ballot this year. About a third of all the recent rating changes by Inside Elections came from the Hawkeye State alone.

According to statewide and district-level data, Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand is well positioned in the race for governor against Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Democrats haven’t won a gubernatorial race in Iowa in 20 years, but Inside Elections has changed the rating from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic. 

Inside Elections has also shifted Iowa’s open Senate race from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican. Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek is running even with or slightly behind GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, but, with lower statewide name identification, he’s got room to grow and could benefit from Sand’s performance on the ballot. 

Iowa’s 3rd District, where GOP Zach Nunn faces Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, has shifted from Tilt Republican to Toss-up. And Iowa’s 2nd District, which Hinson is leaving to run for the Senate, has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. Republican former state Rep. Joe Mitchell faces a tough environment as he tries to hold off Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James. The race for the 1st District, where GOP Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces Democratic former state Rep. Christina Bohannan, continues to be rated a Toss-up, but that rating feels generous to the congresswoman and could be shifting to the Democratic column soon. 

In other Senate races, Democrats have a narrow but distinct advantage in two races at the core of the battleground. Both Georgia (where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff faces GOP Rep. Mike Collins) and North Carolina (where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley are squaring off) have shifted from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic. That leaves Michigan as the only Toss-up Senate contest, according to Inside Elections — for now. 

In Texas, the Senate race shifts from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. A couple of decades of nonstop statewide losses doesn’t mean Democratic state Rep. James Talarico can’t win this year. Polling shows him running mostly ahead of state Attorney General Ken Paxton, but if Republicans make enough of a financial investment, they might be able to consolidate the GOP vote enough to drag Paxton across the finish line.

Texas Democrats haven’t come anywhere close to winning a gubernatorial race since Ann Richards lost reelection to Republican George W. Bush in 1994. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa is making GOP Gov. Greg Abbott work for a fourth term. The state legislator hasn’t raised as much money as Talarico or former Senate and gubernatorial candidate Beto O’Rourke, but the political environment is better. That race shifts from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. 

But there’s some good news for Republicans. In Kansas, outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s preferred choice lost in the primary, and Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson is the favorite to succeed her in November. That race is shifting from Toss-up to Tilt Republican. 

There have been two other recent rating changes in House races. 

In Michigan’s 8th District, national Republicans’ preferred challenger, Navy veteran Amir Hassan, lost the primary, despite having Trump’s endorsement. Instead, GOP voters nominated a candidate who had previously suspended his bid and didn’t have a campaign website when he won the primary. And while Trump finished ahead of Kamala Harris in the district in 2024, Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald-Rivet had $4.2 million in the bank on July 15 and has the national environment in her favor this cycle. This race has shifted from Likely Democratic to Solid Democratic. 

Finally, in Ohio’s 7th District, the combination of domestic abuse allegations against GOP Rep. Max Miller, his refusal to drop out of the race and the overall mood of the electorate gives Democrats a surprise chance of flipping the seat. Until the dust settles a little, the race is shifting from Lean Republican to Toss-up. 

Here’s a summary of the 11 race rating changes: 

Moving in Republicans' favor

Kansas Governor (Open; Laura Kelly, D, term-limited): from Toss-up to Tilt Republican

Moving in Democrats' favor

Georgia Senate (Jon Ossoff, D): from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic

North Carolina Senate (Open; Thom Tillis, R, not seeking reelection): from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic

Texas Senate (Open; John Cornyn, R, lost in primary): from Likely Republican to Lean Republican

Iowa Senate (Open; Joni Ernst, R, not seeking reelection): from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican

Ohio’s 7th District (Max Miller, R): from Lean Republican to Toss-up

Iowa’s 3rd District (Zach Nunn, R): from Tilt Republican to to Toss-up

Iowa’s 2nd District (Open; Ashley Hinson, R, running for Senate): from Likely Republican to Lean Republican

Michigan’s 8th District (Kristen McDonald-Rivet, D): from Likely Democratic to Solid Democratic

Iowa Governor (Open; Kim Reynolds, R, not seeking reelection): from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic

Texas Governor (Greg Abbott, R): from Solid Republican to Likely Republican
